{{short description|American computer scientist}}
[[File:Yuri Gurevich ETH Zurich cropped.JPG|thumb|right|250px|Gurevich at [[Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zürich|ETH Zurich]] in May 2004, photograph by [[Bertrand Meyer]]]]
'''Yuri Gurevich''', [[Professor Emeritus]] at the [[University of Michigan]], is an American [[computer scientist]] and [[mathematician]] and the inventor of [[abstract state machines]].

Gurevich was born and educated in the [[Soviet Union]].<ref name=ylcs>{{Citation |last1=Blass |first1=Andreas |chapter=Yuri, Logic, and Computer Science |date=2010 |chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-642-15025-8_1 |title=Fields of Logic and Computation |volume=6300 |pages=1–48 |editor-last=Blass |editor-first=Andreas |access-date=2023-07-05 |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-15025-8_1 |isbn=978-3-642-15024-1 |last2=Dershowitz |first2=Nachum |last3=Reisig |first3=Wolfgang |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |editor2-last=Dershowitz |editor2-first=Nachum |editor3-last=Reisig |editor3-first=Wolfgang|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> He taught mathematics there and then in [[Israel]] before moving to the [[United States]] in 1982.
The best-known work of his Soviet period is on the ''classical decision problem''.<ref>E. Börger, E. Grädel, and Y. Gurevich. The Classical Decision Problem. Springer, 1997.</ref>
In Israel, Gurevich worked with [[Saharon Shelah]] on
[[Monadic predicate calculus|monadic]] [[Second-order logic|second-order]] [[Theory (mathematical logic)|theories]].<ref>Y. Gurevich. Monadic second-order theories. In J. Barwise and S. Feferman (eds.), Model-Theoretic Logics, Springer, 1985, 479-506.</ref>
The ''Forgetful Determinacy Theorem'' of Gurevich–[[Leo Harrington|Harrington]] is of that period as well.<ref>Y. Gurevich and L. Harrington. Automata, Trees, and Games. STOC '82: Proceedings of the Fourteenth annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing, 1982, 60-65.</ref>

From 1982 to 1998, Gurevich taught [[computer science]] at the [[University of Michigan]], where he started to work on various aspects of computational complexity theory<ref>Y. Gurevich and S. Shelah. Expected computation time for Hamiltonian Path Problem. SIAM Journal on Computing 16:3, 1987, 486-502.</ref>
including average case complexity.<ref>Y. Gurevich. Average case completeness. Journal of Computer and System Sciences 42:3, 1991, 346-398.</ref>
He became one of the founders of the emerging field of [[finite model theory]].<ref>Y. Gurevich. Toward logic tailored for computational complexity. In M Richter et al. (eds.), Computation and Proof Theory. Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1104, 1984, 175-216.</ref>

Most importantly, he became interested in the problem of what an [[algorithm]] is. This led him to the theory of [[abstract state machines]] (ASMs). The ASM Thesis says that, behaviorally, every algorithm is an ASM.<ref>Y. Gurevich. Evolving Algebra 1993: Lipari Guide. In E. Börger (ed.), Specification and Validation Methods, Oxford University Press, 1995, 9–36. https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.06255</ref>
A few convincing axioms enabled derivation of the sequential ASM thesis<ref>Y. Gurevich. Sequential Abstract State Machines capture sequential algorithms. ACM Transactions on Computational Logic 1(1), 2000.</ref>
and the Church–Turing thesis.<ref>N. Dershowitz and Y. Gurevich. A natural axiomatization of computability and proof of Church’s Thesis. Bulletin of Symbolic Logic 14:3, 2008, 299-350.</ref>
The ASM thesis has also been proven for some other classes of algorithms.<ref>[[Andreas Blass|A. Blass]] and Y. Gurevich. Abstract State Machines Capture Parallel Algorithms. ACM Transactions on Computational Logic 4(4), 2003, 578–651, and 9(3), 2008, article 19.</ref><ref>A. Blass, Y. Gurevich, D. Rosenzweig, and [[Benjamin Rossman|B. Rossman]]. Interactive Small-Step Algorithms II: Abstract State Machines and the Characterization Theorem. Logical Methods in Computer Science 3(4), 2007, paper 4.</ref>

From 1998 to 2018, Gurevich was with [[Microsoft Research]] where he founded a group on Foundations of Software Engineering. The group built [[Spec Explorer]] based on the theory of abstract state machines. The tool was adopted by the [[Microsoft Windows|Windows]] team; a modified version of the tool helped [[Microsoft]] meet the [[European Union]] demands for high-level executable specifications. Later, Gurevich worked with different Microsoft groups on various efficiency, safety, and security issues,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://patents.google.com/?inventor=yuri+gurevich|title = Google Patents}}</ref>
including access control,<ref>A. Blass, Y. Gurevich, M. Moskal, and I. Neeman. Evidential authorization. In S. Nanz (ed), The Future of Software Engineering, Springer 2011, 77–99.</ref>
differential compression,<ref>N. Bjørner, A. Blass, and Y. Gurevich. Content-dependent chunking for differential compression: The local maximum approach. Journal of Computer Systems Science 76(3-4), 2010, 154-203.</ref>
and privacy.<ref>Y. Gurevich, E. Hudis, and J.M. Wing. Inverse privacy. Communications of the ACM 59(7), 2016, 38-42.</ref>

Since 1988, Gurevich has managed the column on Logic in Computer Science in the Bulletin of the European Association for Theoretical Computer Science.<ref name=ylcs/> Since 2013 Gurevich has worked primarily on 
[[quantum computing]],<ref>A. Bocharov, Y. Gurevich, and [[Krysta Svore|K.M. Svore]]. Efficient decomposition of single-qubit gates into V basis circuits. Physical Review A 88:1, 2013.</ref>
while continuing research in his traditional areas.

Gurevich is a 2020 [[American Association for the Advancement of Science|AAAS]] Fellow,<ref>[https://www.aaas.org/news/aaas-announces-leading-scientists-elected-2020-fellows AAAS Fellows], retrieved on Jan 11, 2021.</ref>
a 1997 [[ACM Fellow]],<ref>[https://fellows.acm.org/fellow_citation.cfm?id=2256485&srt=alpha&alpha=G ACM Fellows], [[Association for Computing Machinery]]. Accessed February 16, 2010.</ref>
a 1995 [[Guggenheim Fellowship|Guggenheim Fellow]],<ref>[http://www.gf.org/fellows/all?index=g&page=20 Fellows List], {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110622011106/http://www.gf.org/fellows/all?index=g&page=20 |date=June 22, 2011 }} [[John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation]]. Accessed February 16, 2010.</ref>
an inaugural fellow of the [[European Association for Theoretical Computer Science]],<ref>{{citation|title=EATCS names 2014 fellows|department=Milestones: Computer Science Awards, Appointments|journal=[[Communications of the ACM]]|volume=58|issue=1|date=January 2015|page=24|doi=10.1145/2686734|s2cid=11485095}}</ref>
a member of [[Academia Europaea]], and Dr. [[Honoris Causa]] of [[Hasselt University]] in [[Belgium]] and of [[Ural State University]] in [[Russia]].
